questions.stem: What makes up the thermal energy of an object?
options: Only the potential energy stored in the bonds between its particles
The energy it will give out when it cools to absolute zero
The kinetic and potential energy of its vibrating particles combined
The kinetic energy of the whole object as it moves through space at speed
questions.explanation: Thermal energy is the combined kinetic energy of the particles' random motion and the potential energy linked to the forces between them. The motion of the whole object is ordinary kinetic energy, not thermal energy.

questions.stem: Object X is at a higher temperature than object Y. What can you conclude about their particles?
options: The particles of X have a higher total thermal energy
The particles of X are larger and more massive than those of Y
The particles of X have more potential energy between them
The particles of X have a higher average kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of an object's particles. It says nothing about total thermal energy, which also depends on how many particles there are, so a cooler but much larger object can hold more thermal energy.

questions.stem: A bath of warm water at 40 °C and a cup of water at 90 °C are compared. Which statement is correct?
options: The cup holds more thermal energy, because its particles have a higher temperature
Both hold the same thermal energy, because both contain only liquid water at rest
The bath has the higher temperature, because it holds more energy
The bath can hold more thermal energy, though its particles move more slowly on average
questions.explanation: Thermal energy depends on the number of particles as well as their average energy, and the bath has far more water. Temperature tracks only the average kinetic energy, which is higher in the cup.

questions.stem: What is absolute zero?
options: The lowest temperature at which any substance can still be a liquid
The lowest possible temperature, where particles have their minimum energy
The temperature at which pure water freezes at normal air pressure
The temperature of deep space, far from the warmth of any star or planet
questions.explanation: As temperature falls, the average kinetic energy of particles falls until it reaches a minimum at absolute zero, 0 K or about −273 °C. Water freezes at 0 °C, which is 273 K, far above absolute zero.

questions.stem: Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K. What is this temperature in degrees Celsius? Use T(K) = T(°C) + 273.
questions.explanation: T(°C) = T(K) − 273 = 77 − 273 = −196 °C. Adding 273 instead of subtracting gives 350, which would be far hotter than boiling water.

questions.stem: Normal body temperature is about 37 °C. What is this on the Fahrenheit scale? Use T(°F) = (9/5)T(°C) + 32.
questions.explanation: (9/5) × 37 = 66.6, and adding 32 gives 98.6 °F. Leaving out the 32 gives 66.6 °F, and multiplying by 5/9 instead of 9/5 gives about 52.6 °F.

questions.stem: The temperature of a cup of tea falls by 25 °C as it cools. What is the fall in temperature in kelvin?
questions.explanation: One kelvin is the same size as one degree Celsius; the scales differ only in where zero is. A temperature change therefore has the same number on both scales, so the fall is 25 K.

questions.stem: What is heat?
options: The temperature of an object measured on the Kelvin scale
Energy that flows from a hotter object to a cooler one because of their temperature difference
The total amount of thermal energy contained in a hot object at any one moment
A fluid substance that moves out of hot objects into cold objects when they touch
questions.explanation: In physics, heat is energy in transit, flowing from a region of higher temperature to one of lower temperature. An object contains thermal energy, not heat. The old idea of heat as a fluid substance, caloric, was abandoned.

questions.stem: A hot metal spoon is placed in a glass of cool water and left. What happens until thermal equilibrium is reached?
options: Cold flows from the water into the spoon until both hold equal energy
Energy flows from spoon to water until both hold equal thermal energy
Energy flows both ways equally, so neither temperature changes at all
Energy flows from spoon to water until both reach the same temperature
questions.explanation: Energy flows from the hotter spoon to the cooler water until their temperatures are equal, which is thermal equilibrium. They then have the same temperature, not the same thermal energy, because their masses and materials differ.

questions.stem: Why are metals good thermal conductors?
options: Their free electrons carry energy quickly through the material
Their atoms are free to flow around, carrying energy as currents
They emit far more infrared radiation than other solids do
Their particles are spread far apart, so energy moves easily
questions.explanation: In conduction, energy passes through a material by particle collisions. Metals also have free electrons that move through the lattice and transfer energy rapidly. Flowing currents of particles are convection, which needs a fluid.

questions.stem: Why does a room heater placed near the floor warm the whole room?
options: Infrared radiation from the heater travels only upwards through the air
Heated air expands, becomes less dense and rises, setting up a convection current
Heat naturally rises, so it moves straight up from the heater towards the ceiling
The floor conducts energy from the heater up through the walls to the ceiling
questions.explanation: Air near the heater warms, expands and becomes less dense, so it rises and cooler, denser air sinks to replace it. This circulating convection current carries energy around the room. It is the warm air that rises, not heat itself.

questions.stem: Energy from the Sun reaches Earth across about 150 million kilometres of near-vacuum. How is it transferred?
options: By conduction and convection working together
By radiation, as electromagnetic waves need no medium
By conduction, through particles colliding in space
By convection, through currents of gas in space
questions.explanation: Radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves, mainly infrared and visible light, and it can cross a vacuum. Conduction and convection both need particles, which are almost absent between the Sun and Earth.

questions.stem: A vacuum flask keeps a drink hot. How does the vacuum between its double walls help?
options: It reflects infrared radiation back towards the drink
It absorbs the thermal energy that escapes from the hot drink
It stops conduction and convection, which both need particles
It stops radiation, which cannot cross a completely empty space
questions.explanation: With almost no particles between the walls, energy cannot be conducted or carried by convection across the gap. The silvered wall surfaces deal with radiation by reflecting it, because radiation does cross a vacuum.

questions.stem: Why does a down quilt keep a sleeper warm?
options: Down feathers produce their own thermal energy when compressed by the body
The feathers reflect all the infrared radiation emitted by the sleeper's body
Down conducts energy back into the body faster than the surrounding air conducts it away
The feathers trap air, a poor conductor, and stop it forming convection currents
questions.explanation: Still air is a very poor conductor, and trapping it in small pockets between feathers prevents convection. Energy therefore leaves the body only slowly. The quilt adds no energy; it only slows the loss.

questions.stem: Two identical cans of water, one painted matt black and one shiny silver, are left in the sun. Which warms faster and why?
options: Neither, because the water in each can is identical
The black can, because dark matt surfaces absorb radiation better
The silver can, because shiny metal surfaces absorb more of the radiation
The black can, because dark surfaces conduct energy better
questions.explanation: Dark, matt surfaces are good absorbers and good emitters of radiation, while shiny surfaces reflect most of it. The black can absorbs more of the Sun's radiation and warms faster.

questions.stem: Water near the top of a test tube is boiled while ice held at the bottom does not melt. What does this show?
options: Boiling water has no thermal energy left over to pass to the ice
Water is a poor conductor, and the hot water at the top cannot sink by convection
Ice has a very high specific heat capacity, so it cannot be warmed
Glass is a perfect insulator, so no energy at all can reach the ice at the bottom of the tube
questions.explanation: Hot water is less dense, so it stays at the top and no convection current carries energy down. The only route is conduction through the water, and water conducts poorly, so the ice stays frozen.

questions.stem: Why do most solids, liquids and gases expand when heated?
options: Their particles grow larger as they gain thermal energy
Extra particles are created as the substance gains energy
Their particles move closer together as they gain energy
Their particles move faster and take up more space on average
questions.explanation: Heating increases the average kinetic energy of the particles, so they vibrate or move more vigorously and their average separation increases. The particles themselves do not get bigger.

questions.stem: A bimetallic strip is made of brass, which expands more when heated, bonded to steel. What happens when it is heated?
options: It bends so that the brass is on the outside of the curve
It bends so that the steel is on the outside of the curve
It stays straight but becomes longer along its whole length
It stays straight because the two metals cancel each other out
questions.explanation: The brass lengthens more than the steel, so the strip curves with the longer brass on the outside. Thermostats in irons and kettles use this bending to open or close an electrical contact.

questions.stem: Why are small gaps left at expansion joints along a long road bridge?
options: So the deck can expand on hot days without buckling or cracking
So rainwater can drain through the deck instead of pooling
So the deck can contract on hot days without cracking apart
So the deck can sway in the wind without its supports breaking
questions.explanation: A long steel or concrete deck lengthens noticeably on a hot day. Without gaps the expansion would create huge forces that could buckle the structure. Materials contract, not expand, when they cool.

questions.stem: Which everyday device relies directly on the thermal expansion of a liquid?
options: A refrigerator compressor
A vacuum flask
An electric fan heater
A liquid-in-glass thermometer
questions.explanation: In a liquid-in-glass thermometer, alcohol or mercury expands more than the glass as temperature rises, so the liquid climbs the narrow tube. The tube's narrow bore makes a small expansion visible.

questions.stem: In Q = mcΔT, what does the specific heat capacity c of a substance represent?
options: The energy needed to melt 1 kg of it without changing its temperature
The total thermal energy stored in 1 kg of it at room temperature
The highest temperature 1 kg of it can reach before it changes state
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of it by 1 K
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed per kilogram per kelvin of temperature rise, in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, as in Q = mcΔT. The energy to melt 1 kg at constant temperature is the latent heat of fusion.

questions.stem: How much energy is needed to heat 2.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C? Use c = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water.
questions.explanation: Q = mcΔT = 2.0 × 4180 × 60 = 5.0 × 10⁵ J. Using 80 °C as the temperature change instead of the 60 °C rise gives 6.7 × 10⁵ J.

questions.stem: A 0.50 kg aluminium block absorbs 9.0 × 10³ J of energy. By how much does its temperature rise? Use c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.explanation: ΔT = Q/(mc) = 9000/(0.50 × 900) = 20 K. Forgetting to divide by the mass gives 10 K, and multiplying by the mass instead gives 5.0 K.

questions.stem: Equal masses of water and sand receive the same energy from the Sun. Water's specific heat capacity is about five times that of sand. What happens?
options: Both rise by the same amount, because they receive the same energy
The sand stays cooler, because it stores more energy per kilogram
The sand's temperature rises about five times as much as the water's
The water's temperature rises about five times as much as the sand's
questions.explanation: For equal Q and m, ΔT = Q/(mc), so the temperature rise is inversely proportional to c. Sand, with the smaller c, heats up about five times as much, which is why beach sand gets hot while the sea stays cool.

questions.stem: 0.20 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 0.30 kg of water at 20 °C in an insulated cup. What is the final temperature?
questions.explanation: Energy lost by the hot water equals energy gained by the cold: 0.20 × c × (80 − T) = 0.30 × c × (T − 20). This gives 16 − 0.2T = 0.3T − 6, so T = 44 °C. Simply averaging the two temperatures gives 50 °C, which ignores the different masses.

questions.stem: A 0.10 kg copper block at 100 °C is dropped into 0.20 kg of water at 20 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature? Use c = 390 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for copper and 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water.
questions.explanation: 0.10 × 390 × (100 − T) = 0.20 × 4180 × (T − 20) gives 3900 + 16 720 = 875T, so T ≈ 23.6 °C, about 24 °C. Water's much larger heat capacity means its temperature barely moves while the copper cools a long way.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kW kettle heats 1.5 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. Ignoring losses, about how long does this take? Use c = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Q = mcΔT = 1.5 × 4180 × 80 = 5.0 × 10⁵ J, and t = Q/P = 5.0 × 10⁵/2000 ≈ 250 s, a little over 4 minutes. Using 100 °C instead of the 80 °C rise gives about 310 s.

questions.stem: A 50 W heater runs for 600 s in a 1.0 kg metal block, whose temperature rises from 20 °C to 53 °C. What specific heat capacity does this give, and how will it compare with the true value?
options: About 910 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, higher than the true value because some energy is lost
About 910 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, lower than the true value because some energy is lost
About 570 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, higher than the true value because some energy is lost
About 1.1 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, lower than the true value because some energy is lost
questions.explanation: c = Pt/(mΔT) = (50 × 600)/(1.0 × 33) ≈ 910 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Some of the heater's energy escapes to the surroundings, so less heats the block than assumed and the temperature rise is smaller, making the calculated c too high. This is a systematic error.

questions.stem: While ice is melting at 0 °C, energy is being supplied but the temperature does not rise. What is the energy doing?
options: Breaking bonds between the water molecules to change the state
Increasing the average kinetic energy of the water molecules
Escaping to the surroundings as fast as it is being supplied
Being stored as chemical energy inside each water molecule
questions.explanation: During a change of state the energy supplied, the latent heat, breaks or loosens the bonds between particles rather than speeding them up. Because average kinetic energy is unchanged, the temperature stays constant.

questions.stem: Which changes of state release energy to the surroundings?
options: Condensation and freezing
Melting and boiling
Melting and condensation
Boiling and freezing
questions.explanation: When a gas condenses or a liquid freezes, bonds form between particles and energy is released. Melting and boiling require energy input to break bonds.

questions.stem: How much energy is needed to melt 0.50 kg of ice already at 0 °C? Use L = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ for the latent heat of fusion of ice.
questions.explanation: Q = mL = 0.50 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 1.67 × 10⁵ J. No temperature term is needed because the ice is already at its melting point. Dividing by the mass instead gives 6.68 × 10⁵ J.

questions.stem: How much energy turns 0.10 kg of ice at −10 °C into water at 20 °C? Use c(ice) = 2.10 × 10³ and c(water) = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, and L(fusion) = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Warm the ice: 0.10 × 2100 × 10 = 2100 J. Melt it: 0.10 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 33 400 J. Warm the water: 0.10 × 4180 × 20 = 8360 J. The total is 43 860 J ≈ 4.39 × 10⁴ J; leaving out the melting stage gives only about 1.05 × 10⁴ J.

questions.stem: 0.050 kg of ice at 0 °C is added to 0.30 kg of water at 25 °C in an insulated cup. All the ice melts. What is the final temperature? Use c(water) = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and L(fusion) = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Energy lost by the warm water melts the ice and then warms the meltwater: 0.30 × 4180 × (25 − T) = 0.050 × 3.34 × 10⁵ + 0.050 × 4180 × T. This gives 31 350 − 16 700 = 1463T, so T ≈ 10 °C. Ignoring the latent heat and treating the ice as water at 0 °C gives about 21 °C.

questions.stem: Why does a burn from 10 g of steam at 100 °C do much more damage than one from 10 g of water at 100 °C? Use L(vaporisation) = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.
options: Water at 100 °C cannot release any energy until it has turned to steam
Condensing steam first releases about 2.3 × 10⁴ J of latent heat into the skin
Steam is at a much higher temperature than boiling water at the same pressure
Steam particles are larger, so they carry more kinetic energy into the skin
questions.explanation: When steam condenses on skin it releases its latent heat, Q = mL = 0.010 × 2.26 × 10⁶ ≈ 2.3 × 10⁴ J, before the water even begins to cool. Cooling 10 g of water from 100 °C to 37 °C releases only about 2.6 × 10³ J. Both are at 100 °C.

questions.stem: How does evaporation differ from boiling?
options: Evaporation happens throughout the liquid; boiling happens only at the surface
Evaporation needs energy supplied from outside; boiling happens without any energy input at all
Evaporation occurs only above the boiling point; boiling occurs at any temperature below it
Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature; boiling happens throughout at the boiling point
questions.explanation: In evaporation, only the fastest surface particles escape, and it happens at any temperature. In boiling, vapour bubbles form throughout the liquid, which happens only at the boiling point.

questions.stem: Using the particle model, why does sweating cool the body?
options: The sweat conducts energy into the skin, which then radiates it away
The slowest molecules escape as vapour, carrying most of the thermal energy away with them
Sweat has a low specific heat capacity, so it absorbs energy without warming
The fastest molecules escape as vapour, lowering the average kinetic energy of those left
questions.explanation: Evaporation removes the most energetic molecules from the surface. The average kinetic energy of the remaining sweat falls, so it cools and draws energy from the skin. The energy taken is the latent heat of vaporisation.

questions.stem: Solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) turns straight into a gas at normal air pressure. What is this change called?
options: Sublimation
Deposition
Evaporation
Condensation
questions.explanation: Sublimation is the change from solid directly to gas without passing through the liquid state. The reverse change, gas straight to solid as when frost forms, is deposition.

questions.stem: A 100 W heater is placed in 0.10 kg of crushed ice at 0 °C. The temperature stays at 0 °C for 334 s before rising. Ignoring losses, what latent heat of fusion does this give?
questions.explanation: The energy supplied during melting is Q = Pt = 100 × 334 = 3.34 × 10⁴ J, and L = Q/m = 3.34 × 10⁴/0.10 = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Forgetting to divide by the mass leaves 3.34 × 10⁴, which is the energy, not the latent heat.

questions.stem: On a heating curve of temperature against time for a substance heated at a steady rate, what do the flat sections show?
options: Times when the specific heat capacity becomes zero
Changes of state, where the particles speed up suddenly
Changes of state, where energy goes into breaking bonds
Times when the heater was briefly switched off
questions.explanation: The flat sections are the melting and boiling points, where energy supplied as latent heat breaks bonds without raising the temperature. Sloping sections are where the temperature rises according to Q = mcΔT.
